To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ability to relocate patches of high quality resource is a learned behaviour in A. vulgate.
the ability of A. vulgate to find and exploit high-quality food resources increases with time spent foraging in heterogeneous environments.

1) A. vulgale can relocate the position of patches of high-quality food over time; 2) the ability to relocate the high quality food patches is associated with increased consumption rates, growth and survivorship; and 3) the ability to locate high quality food patches in a spatially complex environment may increase the fitness of A. vulgara.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ability of saprophagous macrodecomposers to exploit patchy food resources in the soil.
how animals can use the information they obtain while foraging in heterogeneous environments to increase their fitness.
the fitness consequences of the ability to relocate food in a spatial environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fitness consequences of feeding on spatially heterogeneous environments were not as predicted from the behavioural experiments.

, in the absence of other information on the fitness correlates of foraging behaviour, the ability of A. vulgate to relocate patches of high quality resources may be an important fitness correlate of foraging behaviour.
A. vulgate can relocate patches of high quality resources, but the ability to relocate patches of high food quality is not necessarily linked with fitness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fitness benefits for saprophytes of developing the ability for spatial learning, in order to relocate high quality resources, may be small.
A. vulg are is able to relocate high quality resources, but that this does not necessarily translate into increased fitness in a spatially heterogeneou s environment.
A. vulg are can develop the ability, with time, to relocate high quality resource patches while foraging on patchily distributed food.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while it is important to understand how the spatial distribution of high and low quality food patches affects foraging behaviour, this may not always translate into differences in fitness.

, in contrast to what has been reported for other organisms, A. vulgares fitness is not negatively affected by foraging in a spatially complex environment, and that the ability to relocate food patches is not required for A. vulgarse to achieve a high fitness.

, while A. vulgares can learn to find high quality food patches in low quality food environments, they are not able to use this information to increase their consumption, growth or survival rates in these environments.
